title: Why Colombia Fell for Bre-B
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_text: The guy selling arepas de choclo outside my hostel in Medellín had a laminated card clipped to his cart. No prices on it. Just a QR code and a phone number written in marker underneath. When I held out a 20,000-peso note he took it, sure — but the three Colombians ahead of me in line never reached for a wallet. They scanned, typed, showed him the confirmation screen, and walked off chewing. Eighteen months ago that transaction would have depended on which app everybody happened to use. Nequi customer, Daviplata vendor? Awkward. Today it doesn't matter, and the reason is a piece of infrastructure most travelers have never heard of: Bre-B . Colombia Was a Cash Country. Then It Wasn't. Here's the part that makes the speed genuinely strange. As recently as 2023, cash was still the preferred payment method for almost four out of five Colombian adults. This was not a country itching to go digital. Wallets like Nequi and Daviplata were huge — Nequi alone counts around 25 million users — but they were islands. Sending money between them was clumsy, and paying a merchant usually meant being on the same app they were. Then, on October 6, 2025, the Banco de la República flipped the switch on Bre-B, its interoperable instant payment system. Within six months it had blown past 100 million registered payment keys, with more than 34 million users and over 600 million transactions processed. In a country of about 52 million people, that's not adoption. That's a stampede. ColombiaOne What a "Llave" Actually Is Bre-B runs on llaves — keys. Instead of sharing a 16-digit account number, a Colombian links their phone number, national ID, email, or a custom alphanumeric tag to their bank or wallet account. To get paid, they give you their key. To pay, you type it in or scan a QR that carries it. The money moves in seconds, any hour, any day, and it costs the user nothing. If that sounds like Pix in Brazil , it should — the central bank started designing Bre-B in 2022, openly inspired by Pix's success, with 24/7 transactions and full interoperability as the goal from day one. Colombia watched its neighbor rewire an economy and decided to skip the decade of fragmentation and go straight to the good part. It's the same leapfrog logic we've written about in Southeast Asia : when card infrastructure never fully arrived, there's nothing to protect and no reason to wait. EBANX One Button in Every App The genius move was where they put it. Bre-B isn't a separate app you download. It's a button — a purple "Bre-B" zone that appeared inside Bancolombia, Nequi, Daviplata, Nu, and every other participating bank and wallet, more or less overnight. Over 170 institutions plugged in. Grandma didn't have to learn new software; the app she already had simply started talking to everyone else's. That's why the arepa guy doesn't care what's on your phone anymore. His QR works with all of it. The central bank even picked up a Central Banking award in 2026 for how cleanly the rollout landed — a sentence I never expected to type about payments infrastructure, but here we are. Merchants Did the Math Immediately Card terminals in Colombia are expensive, slow to settle, and take a real bite out of every sale. Bre-B transfers land instantly and cost small merchants essentially nothing. So the tiendas , the fruit stalls, the taxi drivers, the woman selling tintos from a thermos on the Transmilenio platform — they didn't need convincing. Print the code, tape it up, done. The average Bre-B transaction runs around 157,000 pesos, roughly $43, but plenty are far smaller. This is a rail people use for a 3,000-peso coffee without thinking twice, which is exactly the behavior that killed cash-first culture in Brazil, Argentina , and Peru before it. The Tourist Problem, Again And now the familiar catch. Nequi, Daviplata, and the Bre-B button inside every Colombian bank app all require what tourists don't have: a cédula , a local phone plan, a Colombian bank account. You can watch the entire country scan its way through the day while your foreign Visa gets declined at a market stall and the nearest ATM charges you 26,000 pesos for the privilege of withdrawing cash, before your own bank piles on. This is exactly the gap Moreta Pay was built to close . Since launching across Latin America , the whole point has been letting you scan the same local QR codes residents use — no cédula, no local account, no "¿tienes efectivo?" standoff. You top up in your own currency, see the live peso rate before you confirm, and the vendor gets paid like you're any other local. Same wallet handles Pix in Brazil and Yape in Peru, so one top-up covers the whole trip down the Andes. One habit worth stealing from Colombians while you're there: check the recipient name on screen before you confirm. Any payment system that grows this fast attracts fake-QR sticker scams, and a two-second glance is all the protection you need. The Takeaway Colombia didn't drift into digital payments. The central bank built one shared rail, dropped it into every app in the country at once, and a cash-loving nation registered a hundred million keys before the system's first birthday. The arepa cart has better payment tech than most airport duty-free shops now. Show up ready to scan, and Colombia is one of the easiest countries in the Americas to spend money in. Show up with only plastic, and you'll spend your trip hunting ATMs while everyone around you pays with a key.

title: Referral Programs vs. Loyalty Programs: 6 Differences to Help You Decide Which to Build First
summary: Compare referral program vs loyalty program, explore six key differences, and discover which strategy best supports sustainable business growth.
body_text: Define your primary goal: Do you need more customers, more repeat visits, or lower acquisition costs? Your answer points toward referrals or loyalty. Evaluate your existing customer base: Look at repeat purchase frequency, satisfaction, and how often customers already recommend you. If they’re already spreading the word naturally, a referral program can build on that. If repeat purchases are inconsistent, loyalty may deliver better returns. Assess purchase frequency: Businesses with frequent purchases, such as retailers and healthcare providers offering recurring services, often see quicker returns from loyalty programs. Manufacturing businesses with longer sales cycles may benefit more from referral programs instead. Consider budget and technology: Before launching either program, confirm you have a clear reward structure, incentive budget, customer data for personalization, and a platform to automate tracking. Plan for future integration: Most organizations start with one program based on immediate priorities and add the other as customer relationships mature. Our guide on how to build a customer loyalty program walks through that second phase in detail.

title: How to Use JFrog CLI Without Editing Your CI Scripts
summary: Stop editing CI scripts! Use JFrog CLI with your native package commands by setting package_alias=true. Get faster builds and Xray security scanning without friction.
body_text: Using JFrog CLI used to come with a catch. To run a build through it, you had to put it in front of the command. For example, jf npm install instead of npm install or jf mvn package instead of mvn package per the example below: npm install → jf npm install mvn package → jf mvn package Doing that once is easy enough. But across dozens of pipelines, and again with every new project, it adds up to CI scripts you have to keep editing, which becomes yet another responsibility of the overtasked DevOps team. JFrog CLI has now done away with the jf prefix . By setting the parameter: package_alias=true When you set up the JFrog CLI, it overrides your native package-manager’s commands and runs the right JFrog CLI command underneath. No jf prefix is needed and there are no changes to your build scripts. You update the parameter once and never think about it again. Note: When customers are using the native package tool wrapper like mvnw & gradlew in those cases package_alias wouldn’t work as those wrappers point to the absolute path of binaries. Key takeaway: What concerned teams was never the CLI itself, rather it was the CI script changes it used to require. The JFrog CLI now deletes that step by setting one parameter when you install it in the setup process. First, it leaves your build commands as they are. Second, you benefit from faster transfers, a single sign-in, and the build data JFrog Xray needs to scan. Three examples of JFrog CLI requiring script editing The friction between the ease-of-use and efficiency of JFrog CLI and the need for script editing should be considered from the perspective of various users: You’re new to JFrog. You’re wiring up your first pipeline and discover that “use the CLI” means rewriting commands you already know how to run. You’re adopting a new package type. For example, a project that was Maven-only starts pulling in npm or Go, and suddenly the CI scripts need another round of edits to keep CLI coverage intact. You want to turn on security scanning. JFrog Xray checks every package in a build for vulnerabilities and license issues, but first it needs the build data that records what’s in the build. Producing that data used to require significant edits to the CLI script. In every case the blocker was the same: Using JFrog CLI meant changing the scripts. No more! From now on, JFrog CLI removes that blocker entirely. Running native package commands through JFrog CLI With package_alias=true configured at setup, a build step that runs npm install , for example, goes through the JFrog CLI, which runs the matching CLI operation and passes control back to the native tool. A few things make it safe to roll out widely: It coexists with what you already have. Existing jf -prefixed commands keep working with no conflict, so you can turn on this feature without auditing legacy scripts first. New package manager types need zero updates. Adopt a new package manager later and there’s nothing to change. Just bring your native commands as is. The JFrog CLI covers it automatically, so your CI scripts stop being a maintenance item every time your stack grows. You set it once at installation, not on every command. Maintenance becomes a non-issue, with nothing added to your development workflow. Example: How to set up JFrog CLI for GitHub Actions In GitHub Actions, that switch lives on the setup step: jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up the JFrog CLI (Frictionless CLI on) uses: jfrog/setup-jfrog-cli@v4 with: package_alias: true # one switch — no jf prefixes anywhere below env: JF_URL: ${{ secrets.JFROG_URL }} JF_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.JFROG_ACCESS_TOKEN }} - name: Build run: | npm install npm run build Notice the build step, it is a plain npm install , with no prefix and no JFrog-specific syntax. The pipeline looks like any other. It just does more behind the scenes. What is JFrog Build-Info, and how does it empower JFrog Xray? Behind the scenes, JFrog CLI generates Build-Info . This is the essential data that it records including your dependencies, the machine and CI process that produced the build, and more. This crucial metadata, regarding your assets and how they were created, is JFrog’s way of defining, structuring, and capturing all of that data into one consistent record — and JFrog CLI is the tool that is responsible for producing it. Your application security relies on this Build-Info as this is what JFrog Xray reads for vulnerabilities and licensing issues. So with JFrog CLI in place, turning on scanning stops being a scripting project. The data Xray needs is already being generated, with nothing added to your code. Scanning becomes something you switch on rather than a project you need to manage. For GitHub Actions, there’s an added benefit as the build name and number are captured automatically from the runner, so you don’t need to input them manually into the script. What else can JFrog CLI do? Build metadata is only one benefit of letting JFrog CLI handle your commands. There are several more key features and none of them require editing your scripts: Parallel, chunked uploads. Large artifacts, such as a 10 GB file, are split into chunks and transferred in parallel, which is markedly faster than pushing them through the REST API. Persistent authentication. Log in once and keep working; you don’t need to re-authenticate every time you switch repositories or integrations. Broad ecosystem coverage. JFrog CLI supports all the major repositories in the package-manager ecosystem, covering more than 20 leading package types. So whatever your teams build with, JFrog CLI has you covered. Available to everyone. JFrog CLI is included on every JFrog licensing tier and available as an open source package on GitHub . How do you get started with JFrog CLI? JFrog CLI reframes the resources required to adopt or expand the JFrog Platform . New developers get to use the same familiar open source commands that they always have. Existing teams can add packages without additional scripting. And in terms of security scanning, the build metadata JFrog Xray needs to secure your software supply chain is already there. See our download page and read the JFrog CLI documentation to get started, or talk to our team about how to roll it out across your entire development ecosystem.
